title: Canada Political Compass Test 2026 | CoreOpinion
desc: Where do you stand in Canadian politics? 70 statements to see your alignment with the Liberals, Conservatives, NDP, Greens, Bloc Québécois and PPC, plus your framing bias.
keywords: Canadian political quiz, Canada political compass test, Liberal Conservative NDP quiz, where do I stand in Canadian politics, political alignment test Canada, which party should I vote for Canada, Carney Poilievre quiz, Canadian election 2025 quiz

lib.name: Liberal
lib.desc: Your answers most closely match the Liberal Party. You tend to support managed trade, social programs, climate action, and a strong federal role in the economy.

con.name: Conservative
con.desc: Your answers most closely match the Conservative Party. You favour lower taxes, smaller government, axing the carbon tax, and reducing federal spending.

ndp.name: NDP
ndp.desc: Your answers most closely match the NDP. You support pharmacare, dental care, workers rights, wealth taxes, and a more activist government on inequality and climate.

grn.name: Green
grn.desc: Your answers most closely match the Green Party. You prioritise strong climate action, proportional representation, and a systemic challenge to corporate power.

blq.name: Bloc Québécois
blq.desc: Your answers most closely match the Bloc. You support Quebec autonomy, French language protection, and a centre-left social model on federal matters.

ppc.name: PPC
ppc.desc: Your answers most closely match the PPC. You want radical cuts to immigration, elimination of climate policy, and a rejection of mainstream conservative incrementalism.

bank.q: Canada’s public healthcare must stay universal, and private, pay-for-service care should be resisted.
bank.ctx: Canada's Medicare provides universal, publicly funded healthcare, and this wants it kept that way, resisting private pay-for-service care. Wait times for procedures and family doctors are a growing strain. The stake is preserving a fully public system as pressure mounts.

bank.q: Public monopoly means endless wait times; more private options would get Canadians treated faster.
bank.ctx: This argues the public monopoly's long wait times could be eased by allowing more private options, as some provinces and European systems do. Critics fear a two-tier system favouring the wealthy. The stake is whether private care would relieve or undermine Medicare.

bank.q: Immigration levels have been far too high and are straining housing and services.
bank.ctx: This argues Canada's recent record-high immigration — driven by ambitious federal targets — has strained housing and healthcare faster than they can cope, a view that grew as rents soared. The stake is whether the pace of immigration outran the country's capacity.

bank.q: Immigration built Canada and remains essential to its economy and future.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-immigration view: that immigration built Canada and remains essential to its economy and ageing workforce, a long-standing national consensus. The stake is immigration's central place in Canada's identity and economy.

bank.q: Canada should sharply cut the number of temporary foreign workers and international students.
bank.ctx: This targets the sharp rise in temporary foreign workers and international students, whose numbers ballooned and who have been linked to housing and wage pressures, prompting federal caps. The stake is whether these temporary inflows should be sharply cut.

bank.q: Temporary workers and students fill real gaps and enrich Canada; scapegoating them is wrong.
bank.ctx: This argues temporary workers and students fill real labour and revenue gaps and enrich Canada, and that blaming them for the housing crisis is scapegoating. The stake is whether they are a problem or a benefit unfairly targeted.

bank.q: The federal carbon tax is a fair, effective way to fight climate change and should stay.
bank.ctx: The federal carbon tax puts a price on fossil fuels to cut emissions, with most revenue rebated to households. This defends it as fair and effective, backed by most economists. The stake is whether carbon pricing is the smart way to fight climate change.

bank.q: The carbon tax is a cash grab that punishes ordinary families and should be axed.
bank.ctx: This attacks the carbon tax as a cost-of-living burden on ordinary families — the Conservative 'axe the tax' campaign — arguing the rebates don't offset the pain. The stake is whether the tax is fair climate policy or a punishing 'cash grab'.

bank.q: Canada should keep expanding oil and gas production and build more pipelines.
bank.ctx: This supports expanding Canada's huge oil and gas industry — centred on Alberta's oil sands — and building more pipelines to get it to market, for jobs and export income. The stake is the future of a sector central to Canada's economy.

bank.q: Canada must wind down fossil fuel expansion and leave more oil in the ground.
bank.ctx: This argues Canada must wind down fossil-fuel expansion and leave more oil in the ground to meet climate goals, even at economic cost to oil-producing regions. The stake is climate action versus a major industry.

bank.q: Governments should build housing directly and intervene hard to bring prices down.
bank.ctx: This supports governments building housing directly and intervening hard to bring down prices, after home costs in cities like Toronto and Vancouver became among the world's least affordable. The stake is how forcefully the state should act on housing.

bank.q: The housing crisis will be fixed by cutting red tape and letting the market build, not by government.
bank.ctx: This argues the housing crisis is best solved by cutting the red tape and zoning rules that block building, and letting the private market build more, not by government construction. The stake is whether government or the market fixes housing.

bank.q: The wealthiest Canadians and big corporations should pay significantly more tax.
bank.ctx: This supports significantly higher taxes on Canada's wealthiest people and big corporations to fund services and reduce inequality. The stake is whether the rich should pay more.

bank.q: Higher taxes on wealth and business just drive investment and talent out of Canada.
bank.ctx: This argues higher taxes on wealth and business drive investment and skilled people to lower-tax places like the US, hurting Canada's competitiveness. The stake is whether taxing the top raises revenue or repels it.

bank.q: National dental care and pharmacare should be expanded, even at high cost.
bank.ctx: This supports expanding new national social programs — public dental care and pharmacare (prescription drug coverage), recently introduced — even at high cost. The stake is extending the welfare state despite budget pressure.

bank.q: Costly new national programs Canada can’t afford will just balloon the deficit.
bank.ctx: This argues Canada cannot afford costly new national programs that will balloon the deficit and debt. The stake is the affordability of expanding social spending.

bank.q: Quebec should become an independent country.
bank.ctx: This supports Quebec, the mainly French-speaking province, becoming an independent country — the cause behind two referendums (1980 and a razor-thin 1995 No vote). The stake is the possible break-up of Canada.

bank.q: Quebec is stronger within Canada, and separation would be an economic and social mistake.
bank.ctx: This opposes Quebec independence, arguing the province is stronger economically and socially within Canada. The stake is keeping the country united.

bank.q: Quebec’s law banning public servants from wearing religious symbols (Bill 21) is legitimate.
bank.ctx: Quebec's Bill 21 bars some public workers — teachers, police, judges — from wearing religious symbols like hijabs, turbans, or kippahs, in the name of secularism. This defends it as legitimate. The stake is state neutrality versus religious freedom.

bank.q: Bill 21 is state discrimination that punishes religious minorities for how they dress.
bank.ctx: This condemns Bill 21 as state discrimination that punishes religious minorities — disproportionately Muslim women — for how they dress. The stake is whether the law is secularism or prejudice.

bank.q: Reconciliation with Indigenous peoples requires major new spending and returning control over land.
bank.ctx: 'Reconciliation' means repairing Canada's relationship with Indigenous peoples after abuses like the residential schools. This supports major new spending and returning control over land and resources. The stake is how far Canada should go to make amends.

bank.q: Reconciliation has become an endless money pit, and Canadians deserve a firm line on cost.
bank.ctx: This argues reconciliation spending has become an open-ended, poorly accountable cost, and Canadians deserve firm limits. The stake is balancing redress for historic wrongs against fiscal control.

bank.q: Canada should keep tightening gun control, including bans on assault-style firearms.
bank.ctx: This supports tighter gun control, including bans on 'assault-style' firearms enacted after mass shootings. The stake is reducing gun violence versus the rights of lawful owners.

bank.q: Gun bans punish law-abiding hunters and sport shooters while doing nothing about criminals.
bank.ctx: This argues gun bans punish law-abiding hunters and sport shooters — important in rural Canada — while doing little about criminals using smuggled guns. The stake is whether the bans target the right people.

bank.q: Canada must stand up to the United States and retaliate against its tariffs, whatever the cost.
bank.ctx: This supports Canada standing up to the United States and retaliating against its tariffs, whatever the cost, amid Trump-era trade threats. The US takes about three-quarters of Canada's exports. The stake is national pride and leverage versus economic dependence.

bank.q: Picking fights with the US is reckless; Canada’s economy depends on getting along with its biggest partner.
bank.ctx: This argues confronting the US is reckless because Canada's economy depends overwhelmingly on trade with its giant neighbour, so getting along is vital. The stake is standing firm versus protecting a crucial relationship.

bank.q: Canada should sharply raise military spending to meet its NATO commitments.
bank.ctx: This supports sharply higher military spending to meet Canada's NATO commitment (2% of GDP), which it has long fallen short of, amid allied pressure. The stake is whether Canada should invest much more in defence.

bank.q: Pouring billions into the military is money better spent on Canadians at home.
bank.ctx: This argues the billions for the military would be better spent on Canadians' domestic needs like health and housing. The stake is priorities between defence and social spending.

bank.q: Safe-supply and decriminalisation are the right, evidence-based response to the drug crisis.
bank.ctx: 'Safe supply' gives drug users regulated drugs to prevent overdoses, and decriminalisation removes penalties for possession — approaches British Columbia trialled amid a deadly opioid crisis. This backs them as evidence-based. The stake is harm reduction versus enabling drug use.

bank.q: Safe-supply experiments flooded communities with drugs and disorder, and should be scrapped.
bank.ctx: This argues those experiments flooded communities with drugs and public disorder and should be scrapped — pointing to BC's partial rollback. The stake is whether harm-reduction policies help or worsen the crisis.

bank.q: Multiculturalism has failed and produced divided communities with little in common.
bank.ctx: This argues multiculturalism — a Canadian official policy since the 1970s — has failed, producing divided communities with little in common. The stake is whether Canada's model of diversity works.

bank.q: Canada’s multiculturalism is a genuine strength and part of its national identity.
bank.ctx: This celebrates multiculturalism as a genuine strength and a defining part of Canadian identity. The stake is whether Canada's diversity is a success to defend.

bank.q: Islam is not compatible with Canadian values.
bank.ctx: This argues Islam clashes with Canadian values — a view aired in integration and security debates. Critics call it prejudice against a diverse community of Canadians. The stake is whether the concern is legitimate or bigoted.

bank.q: Muslim Canadians are full members of society, and their faith deserves equal respect.
bank.ctx: This holds that Muslim Canadians are full members of society whose faith deserves equal respect. The stake is religious equality versus singling out one faith.

bank.q: Some races are simply more intelligent or capable than others.
bank.ctx: This is a statement of racial supremacism — the belief that some races are innately more intelligent or capable than others. It was the ideological engine of Nazism and the Holocaust, and of systems like slavery and apartheid. Modern genetics finds more variation within any racial group than between them, and the idea has no scientific standing.

bank.q: There is no hierarchy of races; the idea is pseudo-science with a shameful history.
bank.ctx: This states the principle of fundamental human equality: that no race is innately superior in intelligence or ability, and that racial hierarchies are discredited pseudo-science with a shameful history behind slavery and apartheid. It is the moral baseline of modern anti-discrimination law.

bank.q: Sentences are too soft; violent and repeat offenders should spend far longer in prison.
bank.ctx: This argues sentences are too soft and that violent and repeat offenders should spend far longer in prison, reflecting Conservative 'tough on crime' policy. The stake is whether harsher punishment improves safety.

bank.q: Locking more people up has never made Canada safer; prevention and rehabilitation do.
bank.ctx: This argues locking more people up has not made Canada safer and that prevention and rehabilitation work better. The stake is what actually reduces crime.

bank.q: Trans people should be able to change their legal gender based on self-identification.
bank.ctx: This supports transgender rights: letting people have the law recognise the gender they identify as and access gender-affirming care. 'Self-identification' laws, used in countries like Ireland and Argentina, allow a legal gender change without medical gatekeeping. The stake is whether gender is defined by identity or by biology.

bank.q: Biological sex is a reality that the law should not let a declaration override.
bank.ctx: This is the 'gender-critical' view: that biological sex is a fixed, binary reality no declaration or surgery can change, and that the law should rest on it — in single-sex spaces, sport, and official data. Associated with feminists like J.K. Rowling, it clashes head-on with the identity-based view.

bank.q: Parents should have more say over what their children are taught about gender and sexuality.
bank.ctx: This argues parents should have more say over what schools teach their children about gender and sexuality — the issue behind 'parental rights' policies in several provinces. The stake is who controls sensitive parts of the curriculum.

bank.q: Curriculum should be set by educators and evidence, not by parental veto over inclusion.
bank.ctx: This argues the curriculum should be set by educators and evidence, not by a parental veto over inclusive teaching that protects LGBTQ students. The stake is parental authority versus professional, inclusive education.

bank.q: Access to abortion is a settled right and should be fully protected.
bank.ctx: This treats abortion as a settled right that must be fully protected. Canada, unusually, has no abortion law at all — it is treated like any medical procedure. The stake is keeping abortion access unrestricted.

bank.q: Abortion ends a human life, and Canada is wrong to have no legal limits at all.
bank.ctx: This argues it is wrong that Canada has no legal limits on abortion whatsoever, and that a human life is at stake, favouring at least some restrictions. The stake is whether the total absence of limits is right.

bank.q: Medical assistance in dying (MAID) is a compassionate right and its access is broadly appropriate.
bank.ctx: MAID (Medical Assistance in Dying) is Canada's assisted-death law, among the world's most permissive. This defends it as compassionate and broadly appropriate. The stake is the right to a chosen death.

bank.q: MAID has expanded dangerously far and now pressures the poor and disabled toward death.
bank.ctx: This argues MAID has expanded dangerously — with proposals to include mental illness — and now risks pushing poor, disabled, or ill people toward death for lack of support. The stake is whether the safeguards have eroded.

bank.q: Workers need stronger unions and rights, and the right to strike should be protected.
bank.ctx: This supports stronger trade unions and worker rights, including protecting the right to strike, after high-profile labour disputes. The stake is the balance of power between workers and employers.

bank.q: Union power drives up costs and holds the economy hostage; strike laws should be tightened.
bank.ctx: This argues union power drives up costs and can hold the economy hostage — as rail or port strikes show — and that strike laws should be tightened. The stake is curbing union power versus protecting workers' leverage.

bank.q: Canada over-regulates its economy; business needs far less red tape and lower taxes.
bank.ctx: This argues Canada over-regulates its economy and that business needs far less red tape and lower taxes to stay competitive, especially against the US. The stake is whether deregulation would spur growth.

bank.q: Cutting regulation just lets corporations off the hook on workers and the environment.
bank.ctx: This argues cutting regulation just lets corporations off the hook on worker safety, consumer protection, and the environment. The stake is whether rules protect people or just burden business.

bank.q: Canada should cut ties with the British monarchy and have its own head of state.
bank.ctx: This supports Canada cutting ties with the British monarchy — King Charles remains head of state — and choosing its own. Support has grown, especially in Quebec. The stake is whether Canada should keep a foreign, hereditary head of state.

bank.q: The Crown is part of Canada’s constitutional stability and should be kept.
bank.ctx: This defends the Crown as part of Canada's stable constitutional order and parliamentary tradition. The stake is the value of keeping the monarchy.

bank.q: Protecting the French language in Quebec justifies strong restrictions on English.
bank.ctx: Quebec's language laws (like Bill 101 and Bill 96) restrict English to protect the French language in a mostly English-speaking continent. This argues that protection justifies strong limits on English. The stake is safeguarding French versus individual language freedom.

bank.q: Language laws that restrict English go too far and trample individual freedom.
bank.ctx: This argues language laws restricting English — on signs, in business, in schooling — go too far and trample individual freedom. The stake is minority-language protection versus personal rights.

bank.q: Canada should replace first-past-the-post with proportional representation.
bank.ctx: This supports replacing first-past-the-post (most votes wins each riding) with proportional representation, so seats better match the national vote — a reform Trudeau promised but dropped. The stake is how fairly votes translate into seats.

bank.q: First-past-the-post gives Canada stable, accountable governments and should be kept.
bank.ctx: This defends first-past-the-post as producing stable, accountable majority governments and a clear local MP, unlike coalition-prone proportional systems. The stake is stability versus proportionality.

bank.q: Open global free trade has made Canada richer and should be defended.
bank.ctx: This defends open global free trade as having made Canada, a major exporter, richer. The stake is the value of economic openness.

bank.q: Free trade hollowed out Canadian manufacturing and left communities behind.
bank.ctx: This argues free trade hollowed out Canadian manufacturing — factory towns in Ontario and Quebec — and left communities behind. The stake is who globalisation left behind.

bank.q: Protecting nature should take priority over new resource projects and development.
bank.ctx: This puts protecting nature ahead of new resource projects — mines, pipelines, dams — and development, prioritising land, water, and Indigenous rights. The stake is conservation versus resource development, a defining Canadian tension.

bank.q: Endless environmental reviews are strangling the projects Canada needs to prosper.
bank.ctx: This argues endless environmental reviews and approvals are strangling the resource and infrastructure projects Canada's economy needs. The stake is whether the process protects nature or blocks prosperity.

bank.q: Immigrants who won’t integrate or adopt Canadian values should not be here.
bank.ctx: This argues immigrants who won't integrate or adopt Canadian values should not be in the country. The stake is how much cultural conformity Canada should expect of newcomers.

bank.q: Demanding cultural conformity betrays the pluralism that defines Canada.
bank.ctx: This argues demanding cultural conformity betrays the pluralism — acceptance of many cultures — that defines Canada. The stake is integration versus Canada's multicultural ideal.

bank.q: Children should be taught pride in Canada’s history, not mainly its wrongs.
bank.ctx: This favours teaching children pride in Canada's history rather than focusing mainly on its wrongs. The stake is what balance schools should strike about the national past.

bank.q: A country that hides its historical wrongs, like residential schools, from students is lying to them.
bank.ctx: This supports teaching hard truths like the residential schools — where Indigenous children were taken from families and abused, with unmarked graves found in 2021 — arguing hiding them misleads students. The stake is honesty about historic wrongs.

bank.q: The unemployed and poor are treated with too much suspicion; the safety net should be stronger.
bank.ctx: This argues the poor and unemployed are treated with too much suspicion and that the safety net should be stronger and easier to access. The stake is how generous and accessible welfare should be.

bank.q: Welfare too easily becomes a trap, and stricter conditions protect taxpayers who fund it.
bank.ctx: This argues welfare can trap people in dependency, and that stricter conditions protect the taxpayers who fund it. The stake is whether conditions on aid help or punish recipients.

bank.q: Long-standing traditions carry the wisdom of generations and should not be discarded lightly.
bank.ctx: This is the conservative philosophy of tradition, associated with Edmund Burke: that long-standing customs and institutions hold the accumulated, hard-won wisdom of generations, so change should be gradual and cautious rather than sweeping away what works for untested ideas.

bank.q: Worshipping tradition just lets the dead govern the living and blocks necessary change.
bank.ctx: This is the progressive reply, in the spirit of Thomas Paine's line that 'the dead should not govern the living': that treating tradition as sacred just lets the prejudices of the past block overdue reform — as appeals to tradition once defended slavery and denying women the vote.

bank.q: A good society depends more on personal responsibility than on government support.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core right-leaning value: that a healthy society depends mainly on individuals taking responsibility for their own choices and lives, and that leaning too heavily on government breeds dependence and saps initiative.

bank.q: Blaming individuals for problems the system creates is how the comfortable excuse others’ suffering.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core left-leaning value: that many hardships — poverty, poor health, joblessness — stem from unfair systems and circumstances beyond personal control, so blaming individuals lets the comfortable ignore problems they benefit from or could help fix.

heroTitle: Where do you stand in Canadian politics?
heroSub: 70 statements on the issues defining Canada right now: healthcare, immigration, the carbon tax, housing, and Quebec. Every position is asked twice with opposite framing, revealing both your party alignment and your framing bias.
partyStripHtml:

context:
Politics in Canada: the landscape behind this test

Canada is a parliamentary federation using first-past-the-post in single-member ridings. Governments are frequently minorities that survive through case-by-case agreements with smaller parties, which gives those parties real leverage without requiring formal coalitions.

The party system

The Liberal Party has governed for more of Canada's history than any other and has traditionally occupied a flexible centre. The Conservative Party, formed from the 2003 merger of the Progressive Conservatives and the Canadian Alliance, holds the centre-right. The New Democratic Party sits to their left and has repeatedly pushed governing parties toward social programmes, most consequentially on public healthcare.

Two parties have no equivalent elsewhere. The Bloc Quebecois runs candidates only in Quebec and advocates for Quebec's interests and sovereignty. The Green Party competes nationally on environmental grounds. Together they make Canadian Parliaments more fragmented than the electoral system alone would suggest.

The cleavages that actually divide voters

Region matters as much as ideology. The Prairie provinces, with economies tied to oil and gas, have grievances about federal energy and equalisation policy that do not map onto a simple left-right line. Quebec's distinct language, civil law tradition, and approach to secularism produce arguments that barely register elsewhere in the country. Ontario's population size means national campaigns are often fought there.

Housing affordability, immigration levels, healthcare capacity, and the balance between resource extraction and climate commitments are the issues that recur across recent campaigns.

How this maps onto the compass

Canadian politics sits left of the United States on economics, with universal public healthcare as settled consensus, while remaining more market-oriented than Nordic social democracy. On social questions the country is broadly permissive, and issues that remain contested south of the border are largely closed here.

This test asks about Canadian policy specifically, including federal-provincial questions that have no American analogue. For the full profiles, see the Canadian party guides.
